author: Ethan Brooks
title: China Spy Case: Witness Statements Released | Government Report
text:
UK Spying Case Collapse Fuels Debate Over China Threat Assessment
The abrupt end to the prosecution of two men accused of spying for China has ignited a political firestorm in the UK, exposing a complex interplay between national security concerns, diplomatic relations, and legal precedent. The case’s collapse centers on the Crown Prosecution Service’s (CPS) inability to secure government evidence explicitly labeling China as a national security threat – a requirement established by a recent legal precedent.
The individuals at the heart of the controversy, Christopher Cash and Christopher Berry, were charged in April 2024 under the Official Secrets Act, accused of gathering and sharing information detrimental to the UK’s safety and interests between December 2021 and February 2023. Both men have denied the allegations.
Government Warnings of Chinese Espionage
The debate was further intensified Wednesday when Downing Street released three witness statements from a senior government official, Matthew Collins, detailing the UK’s assessment of the threat posed by China. The statements, delivered in December 2023, February 2025, and August 2025, consistently warned of extensive Chinese intelligence operations targeting the UK.
In his initial statement from December 2023, Collins asserted that “The Chinese Intelligence Services are highly capable and conduct large scale espionage operations against the UK and other international partners to advance the Chinese state’s interest and harm the interests and security of the UK.” He elaborated in a February 2025 statement that China, while an authoritarian state with differing values, remains a key economic partner, but also represents “the biggest state-based threat to the UK’s economic security.” The August 2025 statement reiterated these concerns, highlighting that China’s “espionage operations threaten the UK’s economic prosperity and resilience, and the integrity of our democratic institutions.”
Collins specifically cited a cyber-attack on the UK electoral commission between 2021 and 2023 as an example of Beijing’s alleged hostile activity. Despite these warnings, the statements also emphasized the government’s commitment to maintaining a “positive economic relationship with China,” recognizing the benefits of bilateral trade and investment.
Political Fallout and Transparency Demands
The release of the statements followed mounting pressure on Labour Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who accused the government of a “cover-up.” Starmer responded by committing to publish the documents in the House of Commons on Wednesday, stating, “Under this government, no minister or special adviser played any role in the provision of evidence.”
The timing of the statements is significant. The first was provided while a Conservative government was in power, while the latter two were submitted after Labour assumed office. This has fueled accusations from the Conservatives that the previous government deliberately avoided formally designating China as a national security threat to avoid damaging relations with Beijing. Labour, however, contends that the prosecution was constrained by the Conservative government’s prior stance on China.
Details of the Alleged Espionage
According to Collins’s initial statement, counter-terrorism police assessed that the Chinese state recruited Berry as an agent, who then enlisted Cash’s assistance. Cash, a parliamentary researcher, had access to the Commons China Research Group (CRG), a body established by Conservative MPs to analyze the UK’s response to China’s growing influence.
The statements detail a July 2022 meeting between Berry and a senior Chinese Communist Party leader. Following this meeting, Cash reportedly sent Berry a message stating, “You’re in spy territory now.” Information gathered was allegedly passed to an individual named “Alex,” believed to be an agent of the Chinese state. The alleged intelligence included insights into potential ministerial appointments, such as Tom Tugendhat, and the likelihood of Jeremy Hunt withdrawing from the Conservative leadership race.
CPS Concerns and Prosecution Collapse
The Director of Public Prosecutions explained that the case collapsed due to the inability to obtain government evidence explicitly identifying China as a national security threat. A precedent set by an earlier spying case mandated such a designation at the time of the alleged offenses.
A government source indicated that Collins believed his statements provided sufficient evidence, pointing to his descriptions of the “increasing Chinese espionage threat posed to the UK.” However, the CPS reportedly did not clearly articulate what further evidence was required to meet the threshold for prosecution. BBC News understands that Collins assumed his third statement would be sufficient.
Cash, in a statement released Wednesday evening, maintained his “complete innocence,” stating he had been placed in an “impossible position” without the opportunity for a public trial. Berry has previously denied spying for China but has not commented since the case was dropped.
The fallout from this case underscores the delicate balance the UK faces in navigating its relationship with China – a nation simultaneously viewed as a vital economic partner and a potential security threat. The debate over the appropriate level of transparency and the definition of national security risks is likely to continue as the UK grapples with the evolving geopolitical landscape.
